name: Hex
summary: A hosted SQL and Python notebook whose cells form a reactive graph and can be published as data apps. It now leads with AI agents that answer questions from semantic models and curated context.
intro: A Hex project is a notebook of SQL, Python, Markdown, chart, pivot, input and other cells that runs in Hex’s cloud. A SQL cell queries a warehouse connection in that warehouse’s own dialect, or queries dataframes and uploaded CSVs with DuckDB (“dataframe SQL”). Its result becomes a variable: by default a pandas dataframe that Python cells can use, or, in query mode, a query of which Hex fetches only 1,000 preview rows and inlines the full SQL as a CTE into downstream warehouse queries (“chained SQL”), so big results stay in the warehouse. Python cells run in a kernel that Hex starts for each notebook, app, scheduled or API session.

Unlike a classic notebook, the project is a graph. Hex infers the links between cells from variable references in Python and SQL, and in its default Auto mode a run updates every downstream and stale cell; running a single cell leaves its dependants marked stale. The same graph powers apps: you pick the inputs, text and output cells to show, publish a version separate from the draft you keep editing, and an input re-runs only the logic downstream of it, while cells the app doesn’t need are skipped. Scheduled runs (at most hourly) and the REST API rerun a published app and can refresh what viewers see.

Hex now positions itself as AI analytics. The Notebook Agent (August 2025) plans and writes chains of SQL and Python cells; Threads (October 2025) lets people who don’t code ask questions in chat, drawing on semantic models, endorsed tables, workspace rules and published apps. Semantic models are authored as YAML in Hex’s Modeling Workbench (a public beta) or synced from dbt MetricFlow, Cube or Snowflake semantic views. Since July 2026, AI use is metered in credits. Hex is independent: it acquired the BI startup Hashboard in April 2025, raised a $70 million Series C in May 2025, and says it has over 2,000 customers.
strengths: SQL and Python in one project: warehouse SQL, DuckDB dataframe SQL and pandas pass results to each other as variables, and chained SQL keeps large results in the warehouse
Reactive execution inferred from the code, so re-runs are predictable and an app’s inputs recompute only the cells downstream of them
One project goes from exploration to a published app, with scheduled runs, notifications and a REST API that Airflow, Dagster or your own code can call
Agents grounded in the workspace: the Notebook Agent and Threads use semantic models (built in Hex or synced from dbt, Cube or Snowflake), endorsed tables and earlier published work
limits: Closed SaaS: projects and kernels run in Hex’s cloud (multi-tenant by default, with EU, single-tenant and HIPAA options), and projects live in Hex rather than in your repo, though they can be exported to Git

Reactivity relies on spotting variable references, so variables created through `globals()` can break re-runs; kernels have hard limits: 25 concurrent per user, a 15-minute idle timeout for app sessions, 60 minutes for scheduled and API runs, 36 hours at most
Priced per editor ($36 a month on Professional, $75 on Team, Enterprise on request), and since July 2026 AI features consume credits; the monthly per-seat grants don’t roll over

Much is plan-gated or in beta: scheduled runs and cron schedules need Team (Professional gets one scheduled run per project), semantic authoring is a public beta on Team and Enterprise, and Databricks metric views are in beta without sync

notes: Larger compute is billed per minute: from $0.32 an hour for Large (16 GB, 2 CPUs) to $2.58 for 4XL (128 GB, 16 CPUs), and $2.93 to $4.06 an hour for an L4 or A10G GPU. Students and educators get Professional free.

story: Barry McCardel, Caitlin Colgrove and Glen Takahashi met while working at Palantir. They started Hex around the turn of 2020 to build the data tool they had always wanted: as analysts and data scientists they jumped between local Python notebooks, BI tools, spreadsheets, SQL scratchpads and scripts, and shared results as copy-pasted charts, emailed CSVs and one-off decks. A $5.5 million seed round led by Amplify Partners followed in 2020, and in March 2021 Hex opened up as a “Data Workspace for teams”: SQL and Python notebooks with real-time multiplayer editing, and an App Builder to turn an analysis into something stakeholders could click through instead of asking for one more cut of the data.

In October 2021 Hex 2.0 replaced top-to-bottom execution with a reactive graph, and Hex announced a $16 million Series A led by Tomasz Tunguz of Redpoint, along with a first dbt integration. A $52 million Series B led by Andreessen Horowitz, with Snowflake and Databricks investing, followed in March 2022, and a $28 million round led by Sequoia in March 2023 arrived with Magic, AI features that wrote SQL from plain language and by 2024 could generate several chained cells at once.

AI then became the company’s centre. In April 2025 Hex acquired Hashboard, whose self-serve BI, semantic modeling and visualization work it set out to bring into Hex, and in May 2025 it raised a $70 million Series C led by Avra, saying over 1,500 teams used it. The Notebook Agent arrived in August 2025 and Threads, conversational analytics introduced by Hashboard’s founder Carlos Aguilar, in October 2025. By July 2026 Hex said agents had overtaken manual cell creation as the main way people worked in it, and moved AI use onto credits.

choices.choice: SQL cells as first-class citizens beside Python
choices.why: Hex’s founders saw most data people as “analytically technical”: technical in how they work, but not software engineers who want to manage environments. Built-in SQL cells with templating and caching, and later dataframe SQL, answered “Python or SQL?” with both.

choices.choice: A reactive graph instead of a linear notebook
choices.why: Shared mutable state in imperative notebooks hurts interpretability, reproducibility and performance. Hex parses each cell’s code, builds a DAG and re-runs dependants, which also lets a published app recompute only what an input touches.

choices.choice: Apps published from the same project
choices.why: Sharing analysis meant screenshots in decks and long message threads. Publishing selected cells as an app, with inputs such as a checkbox or dropdown, lets stakeholders explore without a separate dashboard tool.

choices.choice: Agents built into the workspace, not a standalone chatbot
choices.why: Hashboard had tried wiring an LLM to semantic models and found it didn’t work well enough. Threads reuses the Notebook Agent’s framework and the workspace’s context, and hands off to a notebook when the data team needs to inspect or extend an answer.
